comment_content:
(大概)課程大綱, 我自己寫左一份(中英對照) 下面可以download。
想要份完整既可以喺其他review度搵
1. 小小引言
------------------------------
一如以往, 我為文章篇幅過長而致歉(英文差所以寫中文)
樓下位仁兄isonngky基本上都表明左我對呢個Course既睇法，可以參考下佢既review
對音樂無興趣/感覺的話我就*強烈不建議*去take 呢個course
最大功夫並不是花喺要讀明白D theory度，而係去做ear training
以中小學music 堂為基礎，如果你不是音痴(sorry)，可以哼到D音出黎其實都有大幫助
唔好理人地既身世背景，做好自己，攞A range唔係無可能
------------------------------
2. ABRSM music theory
------------------------------
我自己本身無讀樂理/無玩任何樂器，所以exactly 對應ABRSM 既grading我唔清楚(可以參考樓下其他review)。
不過我報個HUMA2104之前download過ABRSM幾份past paper(grade 5)。我覺得唔係難得好誇張。
以我幾份past paper既小小經驗同睇過官網syllabus，HUMA2104同ABRSM grade 5 不同之處就係*唔需要背*一堆 德文，意大利文 既術語(e.g. Vivace, langsam, largemente, sostenuto, etc.)
------------------------------
3. 除左讀music theory外，呢個course仲要作曲
------------------------------
(*參考*!!)大約地Music theory佔 80% - 85%, 作曲佔 15% - 20%
主要係一曲(Final project, sem尾交)
放心，幾短下，得24小節。一般中等速度(Moderato)大約一至兩分鐘
整個sem, 2-3個月時間會有2份作曲功課係GUIDE住你，慢慢堆疊份final project出黎(雖然佢地都計homework分)
*唔洗擔心*要寫份好似 貝多芬交響曲 咁既世紀大作，只要跟足佢畀你既指示，攞高分唔難。若果做小小畫龍點睛，應該都可以到top甚至滿分。D TA幾好人下
------------------------------
4. 進度chur唔chur既問題
------------------------------
每堂得50分鐘，而且你可能要3個月(一個sem)讀人地半年一年既theory(雖然可能無咁深入)，係的確會緊湊。
大約每一(到兩)堂叫新野，而且都會stack上去，近final會較辛苦。
所以平時無mud時間研究上堂D resource, notes都好，
有聽開歌既，除左聽歌詞以外，都留意下首歌/樂曲既 調性，節奏同配樂，尤其是教左chord(和弦) 之後，尼D都算係ear training既一部分。
------------------------------
5. 要識聽D咩？
------------------------------
最基本既12個音 (C, C#, D, ..., Bb, B)
分辨節奏 (頂多16分音符)
chord(和弦): triads(三和弦), seventh(七和弦)
因為考試會有Rhythm dictation 同melody dictation(我簡稱Melodictation)：打節奏 + TA彈旋律，你負責默寫番出黎放心會彈(幾多次下), 好似50%就當嗰part滿分。亦都有要分辨chord既題目
上堂同tutorial會同你practice, train, 但自己都要落D功夫(上網自己train下)
尼度有個日本網站可以train 節奏: 
https://www.senzoku-online.jp/solfege/rhythmn_js/
考試既level大概會有個網站8級左右
Melodictation 小小tips: 集中寫曬D音，或者係個rhythm先，再處理剩低既手尾，多數都係音階同broken chord，*絕對*唔會好似 ‘忐忑’ 咁痴線😂

comment_content: HUMA 1102 is an introduction to the history of Western art music, from the medieval era to the present day, with an emphasis on the period between Late Middle Ages (14th century) and Romanticism (19th century). Using the last half a millennium of repertoire as its primary point of reference, the course aims to change the way the student hears and understands music. We will explore the foundations of music cognition and acoustics, look at works in their historical and political context, inspect the relationship of music to other art forms, learn analytical listening skills, and try to understand the creative operations and craftsmanship behind music-making. Prior knowledge of music or music theory is not required, and some basics of notation are covered in class.

comment_workload:
If you have studied ABRSM music theory before, congratulations, this is probably one of the lowest workload course you'll ever take in HKUST. Even if it's a long time ago and you may think you've forgotten everything, it'll be very easy to pick up the contents again.
You do still have to put some effort in the final composition, which you will slowly develop through smaller assignments (major key composition -> major+minor key composition -> final project, which is basically harmonization if your previous work is good enough. You may choose to harmonize only the major/minor section or the whole piece). You do not need to be very creative with the composition as they only assess the technical aspects, i.e. use chords that make sense and add some form of texture, no need to think out of the box. I was very fortunate to have friends with experience in compositions and received some feedback from there.
Term paper (min. 350w) is fine as concert recording was provided.
If you have never studied music theory before, good luck. You'll probably have to compete with other students who have already studied music theory before, which is probably over half the class). STEM students may have an easier time with it as most of the stuff are pretty systematic (like intervals, chords, etc.). Some content must be memorized (circle of fifths -> identify key, inversions), and the rest will become much easier.

course_name: Music Theory I: Introduction to Tonal Music
comment_content:
Good course for people with previous music theory background, although certain terms used are from American English (though this may be due to my instructor, e.g. "Half note" US vs "Minum" UK, "Authentic Cadence" US vs "Perfect Cadence" UK). Does not include any component of music performance. 
Discusses fundamental tonal music notation and scales, although it may be a bit fast for people without prior knowledge and experience. Develops music reading and listening skills through weekly rhythmic and pitch dictations during tutorials (not graded). The final project is a 24-bar composition consisting of 8-bar major and minor parallel period in an ABA (which are already composed during the previous homework from before). 
Shaw Auditorium is also a very nice place to study straight after the lecture since it would be earlier with less people.

comment_workload:
The level of workload on this course is highly subjective depending on prior knowledge and ability. 
Some may find the 1 to 2 homework assignments per week doable within 30 minutes if they have at least a few years of experience in performing classical music; others may take more than an hour per homework. 
A lot of the composition in this course depends also on how well you adhere to the composition guidelines to create tonal music (so basically it's not just about making nice-sounding music, there are guidelines outlined by the instructor that should be followed to receive a high grade).
Attendance is also counted towards 15% of your final grade, if your assigned lecture session is early in the morning and you know that you won't be able to make it on campus or wake up that early, avoid this course. 
The difficulty of the midterm and final exam is generally not hard if you listen properly to the lecture content, with our midterm average being a bit higher than 80%. 
You will also be required to attend a concert to write a concert report which is worth 10% of your final grade. 
To summarise, the main difficulty in this course is purely to do with putting preparation into learning about the course requirements and making sure you meet them.

More details:  
[ Midterm and Final Exam ] 45% 
Definitely pay attention to the midterm exam, I didn’t have enough time to check my paper and got kicked out of A range. Meanwhile you will have more than enough time for the final exam. 
Both the midterm and final will have written section (majority%) and music dictation (about 25-30%). 
[ Written ] 
Based on homework. Study and re-do the homework, then practice online, such as: https://www.musictheory.net/exercises 
[ Music Dictation ] 
For midterm, it will be {1.} analytical listening and {2.} rhythm dictation. For final, it will be {1.} analytical listening, {3.} melody dictation and {4.} “Triads”. 
I don’t remember anything for the midterm, but for the final, the listening part accounts for 57 out of 198 points (28.8%). {1.} is worth 27 points, {3.} is worth 20 points, {4.} is worth 10 points. 
{ 1. Analytical Listening } (midterm & final) 
You will need to determine the texture (major or minor), meter (duple or triple) and tonality (homophonic or polyphonic) for about 3-4(?) songs – they are “supposed” to be easy but (ahem ahem). 
A pdf homework with a list of youtube links will be released before the midterm for practice. 
{ 2. Rhythm Dictation } (midterm) 
There is some leeway, you only need around 75% accuracy (? I don’t remember) to get full marks. The tutorials before midterm will be for practicing rhythm dictation, but it is nowhere near enough. 
I spent A LOT of time on this part. It is completely normal to go insane at first, but it will be more manageable over time. 
I used this website for additional practice: https://tonesavvy.com/music-practice-exercise/14/rhythm-dictation-game-eighth-notes/ 
Haven’t tried this website, but it seems to be a good starting point if you are really struggling: https://www.musicca.com/exercises/rhythms 
It is VERY important to establish how you want to write down what you hear from the rhythm. Instead of replacing what you have already written down, it might be better to write it below for the next iteration. Also, filling your blanks with some random gibberish might help you count the beats better. 
{ 3. Melody Dictation } (final) 
There is leeway for this one too, around 50% accuracy (? I have poor memory) to get full marks. 
The rhythm for the melody dictation is easier than the rhythm dictation in midterm, and I think I did pretty well only because of that. I most certainly did not get or barely got the note pitches right. 
I did not study for this part. 🙃 
{ 4. “Triads” } (final) 
This part is to determine the quality of triads by ear (major, minor, diminished, augmented). However, I believe this part is subject to change, as in this could be determine the intervals, chords, or key and scales. 
In the (final?) tutorial, I believe you will have a chance to practice whatever it is that will appear in the final exam. 
I also spent a lot of time on this (arguably too much for a mere 10 points). It is extremely normal to get absolutely everything wrong at first, but practice makes perfect. 
I used this website for practice: https://tonedear.com/ 
[ Final Project + Composition Homework ] 15% 
There are three composition homework, which guides you to your final project. The first is rhythm composition, the second is major melody composition, and the third is minor melody composition. (the first one serves as an introduction separate from the second and third) 
You will get feedback for the homework, and it is very important to ask if you don’t understand. 
The final project is just a harmonization of your composition homework. So long as you do well in your composition homework, your final project shouldn’t be too far off. 
Definitely use a music notation software to help you. I highly recommend using MuseScore 4, it’s lightweight and free. 
[ Concert Report ] 10% 
Attend a concert, then a concert recording will be sent to you. Pick your favorite song and listen to it a few dozen times, then write about it. The concert report is very simple, just write about what you feel when you hear the piece, supported by why (analyze the structure: ABA’ structure? substructure? motifs?; analyze the melody: stable? jumpy?; analyze the quality: loud? soft?) 
p.s. I got ~89% = B+ 🙃🙃🙃 
the mean is 84.50% (might not be the most accurate)
comment_workload:
Speaking from someone who had no prior music theory knowledge (except how to read basic music notations). 
[ Homework ] 
The workload is reasonable. At first it will take quite some time to do the ~2 homework per week (and check it), but you’ll speed up eventually with more practice. 
[ Midterm and Final Exam ] 
There are only a few simple things you need to memorize: the order “FCGDAEB”, placement of sharps and flats in G-clef + F-clef + C-clef, harmonic and melodic minor, Circle of Fifths, notation for harmonic analysis (roman numerals, in major or minor, inversions), and 4 different cadences. It may seem a lot at first glance, but it really isn’t. 
The most time-consuming part of this whole course would be ear training. I spent more time doing ear training than studying the contents, even though the music dictation section doesn’t account for a lot. The rhythm and melody dictation done in the tutorials are much harder than in the actual exam, so don’t dwell on it too much. 
The most effective way to train your ears is to do many short sessions each day (20mins to 1hr each session), instead of jamming everything together in one long session (your brain will get fried), and especially not right before the exams. You WILL feel your brain melting for the first 3-5 days, but if you persist and after a few good nights’ sleep, you will notice substantial improvement. 
The rest of the exams are based on homework, so just study those, do some exercises, and you’re good to go. 
[ Composition Homework + Final Project ] 
Since the final project is based on your composition homework, it doesn’t have much extra workload. 
[ Concert Report ] 
Nothing too difficult. Write 1-2 pages, minimum 350 words (but write more than that, I recommend ~500 or more). 
-----------------------------------------
Don’t be discouraged to take this course. Contrary to other reviews, even if you haven’t studied music theory before, this course is worthwhile. The more time and effort you spend, the more you will learn and transform your ears.

comment_workload:
The workload was absolutely horrible; I was the scriptwriter for the play and it was constant stress. Completely unnecessary!
I came up with the whole story and was genuinely excited to make it with the rest of the class who shared the same enthusiasm as me. However, this excitement quickly turns into disappointment and resentment for this course and for some classmates who made my semester a living hell.
A group of them tried helping me writing the script, however they proceeded to completely rewrite my entire script after I worked a long time on it, thinking very carefully about the dialogue, timing and pacing. The story was all over the place; they didn't care about the message of the story to the audience and instead focused too much on parts of the story that were unnecessary. One of the writers had the role of the main character and made sure that her role was always the center of attention and overly dramatic.
I have encountered way too much drama in this course; the teachers were very absent during those times, despite seeing us confront each other during a meeting, where I complained about the heavy workload that was put on me and other students because of those who ruined the script.
When we finished the play, I felt very relieved to be done with this nightmare. I was mentally and physically tired, and the worst part was that I had to worry about my final exams right after, since we performed on the day the study break began.
However, I can fairly say that I have learned a lot from this course, and you will too if you choose to take it. This course will help you gain confidence in yourself through the art of performing (I can say from experience I also played a character in addition to scriptwriting). In the midst of the drama (in a musical drama, how ironic), I was able to speak up for what I believed was right, so did other students. Many of us will have to face such confrontation in our everyday lives in the future, and this course enables you to get a taste of it with meeting some really obnoxious and arrogant people (hopefully your class won't have bad apples), having to work under constant stress and taking charge of a project when it's going down the wrong path.
If you take this course, I wish you the best of luck. Do not take the role of scriptwriter alone; work with some people who respect your story and you as the creator. Make sure you all agree on the overall strong message you want to convey to the audience and do not get sidetracked by making it look "super dramatic" and "emotional". Think of the core first. That will carry your play, it doesn't have to be impressive! Everyone has priorities, and musical drama is going to be at the bottom of the list so keep it simple.

comment_grading:
You've probably seen the marking scheme already, but just in case, here it is again:
1. Attendance and Participation: 5%
2. Weekly timeline, biographies, notes for readings and documentaries: 20%
3. Film Reviews: 30%
4. Research Paper Outline and Timeline: 10%
5. Research Paper [of someone/thing relatively unknown to most people]: 25%

Here are my grades:
1. Attendance and Participation: Don't know, he actually only took attendance 3 times in the middle of the lecture, so attend all lectures and stay until the end. I probably got full marks.
2. Weekly Timelines: 22.3%
3. Film Reviews: 13.8% + 13.5%
4. Research Paper Outline: 8.5%
5. Research Paper: 25%
6. Rough Cut: Don't know. He went by it really fast. I actually don't know.
7. Final Documentary: 5%
Final grade: A
Some of these reviewers said they did the requirements and still got a D. Just doing those requirements are not enough, they actually go through all of the things in detail.
For instance, in point 2, if you do the same biographies, they will deduct marks. If you copy other people's notes, you get points knocked off. In point 4/5/6/7, if your group is doing someone most people know about, like Mao Zedong, Chiang Kai-shek or others, you're not getting a good score.
It's VERY possible to get a good grade. Even saying pretty random stuff in your film reviews net you an above average score. While points 1 and 6 are never explicitly revealed, those only account for 10%. Doing the essay and the weekly notes well can already net you a great score. Those are just the cherry on top. You have to be insightful and well-researched to get a good grade. Again, just fulfilling quota is not nearly enough.
The professor quite literally showed the ExCel sheet where he kept the marks in the first couple lectures. How are you gonna say it's not transparent at all? Self reporting perhaps?

According to the professor, the A range is ~20% (adjusted for those on the boundary of A range).

As suggested by the course name, this course devotes all of its content to traditional Chinese painting, particularly artistic critique.
Don't worry if you can't draw proper painting or if you didn't take visual arts in high school at all: I can only draw stickmen, and this don't affect my grade at all. *The last lecture was reported to be about the Eight Eccentrics of Yangzhou, but apparently Professor Fu didn't have time to mention them.
*There were also 2 guest lectures by Professor Wu Hong (not from HKUST) on late Qing self-portraits and an painter from Hong Kong Baptist University who demonstrated Chinese painting techniques. Their contents were not examinable in quizzes.
Also a kind reminder for those who want to enroll in this course in the future. As a non LANG course that can fulfil Chinese language common core requirement, this course is extremely popular among students (or "C-LANG refugees"?)
*If you are not in year 4 (and if you are not HUMA student, who have their own quota), please GIVE UP: you'll probably end up in the waiting list at some 100th or 200th position.
*For year 4 students who really want to get into this course, your chance to get into this course entirely depends on careful preparation, mouse clicking speed on SIS and luck.
*I was placed at the 6th place of the waitlist initially, and I only get into the course near the end of the add-drop period. Hopefully this can serve as a useful reference when you are waitlisted.
comment_teaching:
Professor Fu Li-tsui's teaching is probably one of the best in UST, much better than the consistently roasted Chinese LANG instructors. A Taiwanese, her Mandarin/Putonghua accent is impeccable, though you may want to pay extra attention to pronunciation of artist names, like for the artist Guo Xi, I often heard it as "Boxi" (Persia)... Never mind...
Answering questions was encouraged and required (for at least 5 times) during lectures. Don't worry about wrong answers: as Professor Fu would guide you (and the class) to the correct answer nicely and kindly. When Quiz 1 was about to begin, she also calmed us down by suggesting us that "we should probably appreciate these paintings as if they were shown the last time".
Lectures were lively with frequent interactions, though the lecture hall is dark to show the lecture slides containing paintings. Professor Fu was also willing to answer questions after lectures, and I did enjoy discussing some historical backgrounds with her.
For the guest lecturers, Professor Wu Hong delivered his bland lecture in awful Kinabatangan MP English, while the HKBU painter delivered her guest lecture in understandable Mandarin. To be honest, the second guest lecture was much more interesting, as we did see how a Chinese painting was created from abstract elements to a recognizable object.
comment_grading:
Class participation: 5% (Full)
Class attendance: 9% (Full)
Quiz 1: 20% (16.8/20, mean 14.3/20, median 14.4/20)
Quiz 2: 20% (16/20, mean 14.19/20, median 14.5/20)
Group project presentation: 30% (29/30, mean 26.53/30, median 26/30, low 24/30)
Group project written report: 10% (10/10, mean 9.81/10, median 10/10, low 9.5/10)
Group project evaluation: 6% (Unknown)
Class attendance is mandatory, and unlike some LANG courses that allows some leeway, each absence from lecture deducts 1%, and each absence from guest lectures and group project presentations deducts 2%. Every attempt in answering question in lectures or Canvas discussion board would give you 1% (1% max per each lecture/discussion thread) in class participation. While you only need answer questions for 5 times, answering more questions is certainly interesting in the lecture.
There is no doubt that the quizzes, which effectively act as the course's midterm and final exams, can be demanding to some students:
*Quiz 1 was a closed book MC exam with no cheat sheet allowed. The questions would show some cropped out details of paintings and ask related questions like "which of the following(s) is/are created by [artist name]?". You should prepare for very similar objects being shown on a very microscopic scale. My advice is try to catch every details you can observe: line of sight, position of buildings, and even the background (which may have different level of staining).
*The open-book Quiz 2 was about painting critique. There was a short question that gave you an artwork not shown in lecture created by an unknown artist and 3 other known artwork with known artist. Your task was to find out who is the artist based on the similarity and differences. The long question required you to compare two paintings, with subsections asking about differences and similarities before leading you to the overall evaluation.
Speaking of the project, this year's topic was Tradition and Innovation. A 4-5 member group would select a modern artist and compare his/her works with traditional ones to conclude their similarities and differences, to be reported in a 15-minute group presentation and a written report (to be submitted within 1 week after the presentation). As mentioned by someone before, Professor Fu didn't heavily scrutinize the report, which is reflected in the extremely high mean and median.
I was preparing for a B+ to A- grade, but at the end I get an A for this course, which was certainly satisfying with my (and my groupmates') effort. When compared with Chinese LANG's Schrödinger grading, HUMA2660 is certainly a stabilizer for your GPA.
comment_workload:
As mentioned in the grading section, Quiz preparation constituted a significant portion of your workload. You should seriously familiarize with the artists' names and their paintings, at least for the course's first-half (which included some ~40 artists spanning across 5 dynasties!).
The project requires you to study a modern artist, so you may want to arrange your groupmates to visit an arts museum or a painting gallery for the purpose of taking high-resolution images. Alternatively, you may need to find painting collections in the library if there is no collection in Hong Kong (which was the case for my group). I was lucky to be grouped with some experienced groupmates, and overall, a 5-member group would divide smaller individual workload, which is true for busy year-4 students.

HUMA 2680由ancient Greek and Rome到Gothic and Renaissance再到modern architecture，帶你探索喺時間長河入面，西方建築因應當時文化背景同科技發展嘅轉變。因為architecture嘅特色同結構係同當時嘅cultural/religious context息息相關嘅（例如gothic architecture嘅ideal係同宗教相關，信奉God is light同reach God in heaven，所以gothic architecture會pursuit luminosity同verticality），所以上堂嗰陣唔單止學到唔同時代嘅建築特色，仲可以學到少少唔同時代嘅歷史背景、宗教文化等等。

comment_teaching:
Honestly, Cathy is a passionate professor and you can tell from the start of the course. She's just tryna make the class environment supportive and interesting for everyone (that means she'll tell everyone to shut up and listen to her if people keep talking and creating noise, politely). That also means you can always talk to her after class for gaining more understanding on the concepts and assignments and stuff.
She tried her best in every class to be interesting and really, she's just trying to help you at all times. Also she's one of the few professors who actually takes breaks in between, so that's a plus.
Objectively, I think that there are times where the lecture does get boring or vague, because there's just a lot of humanities jargon and sometimes it could also get pretty overwhelming too. However, I don't think it's due to her teaching though, but because of how in Humanities certain people's theories overlap or contradict with each other. Actually if you look at the readings, you'll actually realize how fatally boring the pragmatic theories are when you're simply reading through. This professor has actually made it interesting to learn. I gave up on the readings pretty early on, because the professor makes it much more intuitive and straightforward.
Her English is pretty advanced even for a native speaker myself, so there were times where I struggled to follow her. I realized that it's not that important to know every single concept perfectly though. Anyhow, she is aware when there are tricky concepts and tries to make sure the understanding is clear.

course_name: Contemporary Architecture: The Pritzker Prize Winners
comment_content:
My mum, who is an architect, had a look at my lecture slides and said,
"TOTAL BULLSHIT"
...
Lecture schedule in a nutshell
Weeks 1-6: contribution from INSTRUCTOR
Introducing the history of contemporary architecture, architectural styles and notable architects.
Weeks 7-13: contribution from STUDENTS
Group presentations, report composition, final exam.
See attachment A1 for a detailed breakdown.
See workload part to understand how the assessment works.
...
Two main points:
1. You worship architects in this class.
If you have a great architectural sense and dream, go elsewhere. This is a HUMA course, theories only, nothing practical. You would rather treat all architects as heroic figures and appreciate all of their designs, because they are perfect. The instructor does not explicitly label them as idols of course, but she will be mad if anyone in the audience thinks a design is bad.
2. Keywords, keywords, keywords!!!
You will come across with a lot of names that are specially used to describe an architect's style. However, architects often don't define their styles, or limit themselves to certain styles. From one style to another, there is often no clear boundaries to describe it; but if you miss the keywords, the instructor will be mad again and thinks that you begin to make it up instead of using the keywords she taught.
See the grading part for survival tips regarding this issue.
Overall speaking, the course is eye-opening to understand contemporary architects and architecture. But do your due diligence, you do not have to compliment every single design just because they come from the hands of a starchitect.
comment_teaching:
Three key elements for every lecture:
1. Pictures.
2. Instructor yapping.
3. Student yapping.
I.e. the instructor displays the pictures of a certain work of an architect and introduces its background; if her mood swings, she turns to the crowd and asks for the audience's opinions on the works.
The instructor seems to assume we all are professionals and should analyze very well. So I would recommend you making sure your idea is correct or close before raising your hand to answer a question. She will be mad again if the reply is unsatisfactory. Remember, she will remember your name and reflect your performance on the grades. See more in the grading part.
Nevertheless, the instructor can speak English fluently with very minimal accent. And she pronounces names very precisely, e.g. pronouncing Le Corbusier in a French way, so one should not deny her professional teaching attitude.
comment_grading:
Grade allocation:
25% - Project presentation
25% - Project report
10% - Consultation meetings
20% - Classwork
20% - Attendance and comments on presentations
...
Not hard to get a B range if you obey the seven survival tips below. I got a B- by the way, without following #1, #3 and #4.
1. Form your team CAREFULLY.
Triple check if your teammates can all dedicate certain effort into the project because it can be time-consuming. Also if you know the person very well, only let him/her join your team if he/she is a very responsible person. Remember that 10% of the grade comes from the two consultation meetings with the instructor. ALL members must attend both so if even one of your teammates does not show up, everyone in the team will have marks deducted.
2. Choose Norman Foster, or a Japanese architect.
For the group project this semester, every team has to pick one Pritzker Prize winner for their research question and presentation. Among all, I personally prefer Norman Foster as he should be the architect that has the most projects in Hong Kong so far, so it will be easier to conduct research. You can also consider Japanese architects (e.g. Tadao Ando) because they are the instructor's favourite.
3. Impression matters. Sit on the first two rows.
Your attendance is counted by participating in the discussion every lecture. Make sure the instructor can clearly see your face so she remembers you. You will also have to yell your name to let her mark it down on a piece of paper, so it's better to sit nearer to the stage.
4. Pay extra attention to keywords.
Many keywords mentioned in the lecture does not have a lot of information available online (so I boldly believe that the instructor made them all up). Make sure you listen to how the instructor defines each keyword. You can create a keyword list by category:
- Architectural styles (e.g. deconstructivism)
- Building materials (e.g. béton brut)
- Aesthetic principles (e.g. fukinsei) etc.
5. NEVER leave mid lecture.
We have someone leaving the lecture theatre while the instructor is still speaking. When he leaves and closes the door,
Instructor: "What's his name?"
His teammates: "XXXXX XXXXX"
Instructor: "I will deduct his marks!"
6. Worship your chosen architect at all costs.
Be prepared to optimize all means of research to support the evidence you have gathered about the architect your team has chosen. By saying that, you must rely on not only online resources, but also books, magazines, museum collections, or even course materials from friends who are taking architecture in other universities. If research is not seriously conducted (= online resources only), the instructor is going to be mad.
7. DO NOT trust the instructor.
For the group project, there will be a general guidelines that is of the same version for every team. But note! It is a GENERAL one and if your team directly copies the suggested outline, the instructor is going to be mad because your team fails to customize the presentation according to the architect's story. Even worse if your team does not have a specific research question, which is not explicitly mentioned as well.
comment_workload:
The course is chill for the first few weeks.
But it will be hell for the remaining weeks.
Suggest allocating at least 4-5 hours every day to prepare for the group presentation.
After the presentation, you will be given two weeks to finish up the report, also a groupwork. That also requires a lot of research. Allocate 5-6 hours per day.
Meanwhile do not forget to comment on your coursemates' presentations to earn attendance marks (on a comment form that will be distributed by the TA). Be sure to jot down the keywords from their presentations seriously. Unserious comments will result in 0 mark.
See attachment A2 for the detailed marking criteria and guidelines for research.

comment_content:
先寫一下大家關心的吧，期末考試有四題，大概意思是：
1. 老子的人生論與政治論。
2. 老子說「道沖而用之或不盈。淵兮似萬物之宗。挫其銳 解其紛 和其光 同其塵。湛兮似或存。吾不知誰之子 象帝之先。」。翻譯並論述這段話在老子思想體系中的含意。
3. 逍遙遊主要用哪些寓言故事說明「至人無己，神人無功，聖人無名」的意思，並論述這一主張的含義
4. 養生主論述了莊子什麼養生思想。
評分準則是每題25+8分。25分是內容，8分是表達分，四選三作答。所以滿分是99分。內容分是一個重點一分，有嚴格的marking scheme，不是impression marking，所以不要浪費時間寫自己的見解，而是回答課堂上講過的重點。（課堂上沒講過考試模式是這樣的，相信不少人包括我也寫了很多個人見解）
從marking scheme去看不一定要一字不漏背誦原文，但有些部分幾乎是逐句給分，漏一句都會失分，所以拿高分還是要背誦的。例如第一題政治論有6分就是要解釋「不尚賢，使民不爭」，「不貴難得之貨，使民不為盜」，「不見可欲，使心不亂」，各兩分，不必背原文，但不能籠統的講，必須分述。
雖然第一題人生論通常是指老子的第二章，政治論是第三章，但要是你舉了其他章節有相關人生和政治的也能有分，例如「上善若水」這些，應該算是bonus分數，可以彌補你在第二三章漏掉的分數，我考試時沒有這樣做所以只拿了18/25左右的內容分數。
內容方面，其實上頭幾節課已經把思想說透徹了，後面全部都是重複前面的東西但以不同角度說明，不會讓你有什麼大徹大悟的感覺。可是考試上還是需要你把這些不同角度都記起來才能拿到好分數。道家說「得意忘言」，但考試切記不能這樣。
要拿滿分是很難的，首先你要背得到所有相關原文（至少每一句意思都要記得），然後按照老師課上詮釋的方向解釋而且不能有所缺漏（例如天下皆知美之為美，斯不美矣要用縱橫角度說明，然後再從相對角度說明，共3分），在原文上正確的elaboration也是有分數的。前面四題評分準則我都記下來了，有興趣可以向我購買，雖然這個course不一定會再開了。

course_name: Philosophical Inquiry into the Modern World
comment_content: Content is a brief history of modern western philosophy, from Descartes to a few modern philosophers. The course is split into scientific revolution era philosophers (Descartes, Spinoza, Cavendish, Conway, Leibniz) with a focus on epistemology and metaphysics, enlightenment era philosophers (Hume, Kant, Mill, Dilthey) with a focus on more epistemology, and some modern and contemporary philosophers (Heidegger, Beauvoir, Moore, Wittgenstein, Arendt, Quine, Jaeggi) on truth and identity. Due to the short period of this course, most philosophers only get a couple of lessons dedicated to them, so don't expect a lot of depth and detail on any particular worldview. You should see this as an eye-opener that exposes you to many different flavors of modern philosophy that you can then look deeper into.
comment_teaching: Eric S. Nelson is an excellent philosopher who is great at explaining deep and difficult philosophical concepts. He freely welcomes and encourages students to raise their hands and ask questions in the middle of his lectures, making the class feel more like a discussion group - essential for philosophy. He also spends a lot of time after class explaining to anyone who has questions to ask him - if you take his class, don't be shy to chat with him about anything at all, his passion for philosophy is infectious.
comment_grading: Grading is rather lenient, the professor and the TA don't expect you to be a genius philosopher at this stage. What they do expect is an understanding of the concepts taught in the class, what the abstract words actually mean - if you can do that, you'll get very high marks, and you don't need super high marks to get an A.
comment_workload: There are 3 quizzes that should only take a short amount of study - though this depends on how quickly you can grasp the concepts - and a 2 minute poster presentation at the end that should only take a couple days of work. No final exam with all the concepts, just a quiz after each chapter. By UST standards, this course is a welcome break from literally everything else.
